note: Reviewed explanation prose for MPPSC 2012 Paper I. Exactly the same four-part structure and per-option reasoning standard as the 2013-2024 audits. Unkeyed defective/ambiguous items have no option marked correct; their correct_reasoning explains why no key is assigned. These are independently verified answers, not officially authenticated MPPSC answers.

MPPSC-2012-001.correct_reasoning: NDRI Karnal cloned a buffalo ('Garima-II', a hand-guided cloned calf) after its first buffalo clone Garima, so the animal in the news is buffalo, not sheep or cow. Cloning an animal means producing a genetic copy by nuclear transfer, and NDRI's work used buffalo somatic cells.

option_explanations.reason: The first NDRI clone was a buffalo, and sheep clones such as Dolly belonged to the Roslin Institute in Scotland, so sheep does not fit the Karnal work.
Garima and Garima-II were cloned water buffalo calves produced by the National Dairy Research Institute at Karnal in Haryana, so buffalo is the reported animal.
NDRI's headline clone was a buffalo; cow cloning was reported by other Indian laboratories, not this second clone at Karnal.
Goat was not the species of NDRI's second clone; the institute's cloning programme at Karnal centred on buffalo embryos and calves.

key_concepts: Animal cloning by somatic cell nuclear transfer
NDRI Karnal and Garima-II buffalo clone
Dolly the sheep was a Roslin Institute clone
revision_takeaways: Associate NDRI Karnal with the cloned buffalo Garima and Garima-II.

MPPSC-2012-002.correct_reasoning: Python is a non-venomous constrictor: it kills prey by coiling and suffocation rather than injecting venom. Cobra, viper and coral snake are all venomous snakes with specialised venom glands and fangs, so python is the odd one out.

option_explanations.reason: Cobra is an elapid with potent neurotoxic venom and a hood, so it is decidedly poisonous rather than non-poisonous.
Vipers possess solenoglyphous fangs and haemotoxic venom, so calling a viper non-poisonous is incorrect.
Coral snakes are elapids with dangerous neurotoxic venom despite their small size and bright bands, so they are venomous too.
Python lacks venom glands and subdues prey by constriction, which makes it the non-poisonous snake among these four.

key_concepts: Venomous elapids: cobra and coral snake
Constriction as a non-venomous feeding strategy
revision_takeaways: Separate venomous families (elapids, vipers) from non-venomous constrictors such as python.

MPPSC-2012-003.correct_reasoning: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 at Jim Corbet National Park with nine initial tiger reserves, under Indira Gandhi's government, after the tiger population had fallen sharply. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 provided the legal base, but the dedicated centrally sponsored scheme began in 1973.

option_explanations.reason: 1971 predates both the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 and the tiger census that prompted the Project Tiger scheme, so 1971 is too early.
Project Tiger was formally launched on 1 April 1973 at Jim Corbet National Park with nine founding reserves, so 1973 is the year asked for.
By 1977 Project Tiger was already being expanded to additional reserves, so 1977 is an expansion year rather than the launch year.
1991 is far too late: by then the project had been running for nearly two decades and had many more than nine reserves.

key_concepts: Jim Corbet National Park as the first tiger reserve
revision_takeaways: Remember 1973 for Project Tiger and 1972 for the Wildlife Protection Act, not the other way round.

MPPSC-2012-004.correct_reasoning: An anemometer measures wind speed; the Hindi option says 'पवन वेग' (wind velocity), while the English 'Force of the wind' is an imprecise rendering of the same choice. No other option concerns wind, so C is the intended instrument reading even though the English wording is loose.

option_explanations.reason: Velocity of water-flow is measured with a current meter or pitot tube, not with an anemometer whose cups or vanes respond to moving air.
Depth of water is measured by a sounding line, echo sounder or bathymeter, instruments that have nothing to do with an anemometer's rotating cups.
Force of the wind is the exam's loose English wording for wind speed; the Hindi option gives पवन वेग and the anemometer is the wind-speed instrument.
Intensity of light is measured by a lux meter or photometer, so an anemometer cannot be the instrument for this option.

key_concepts: Anemometer: wind speed, cups or vane
revision_takeaways: Note the translation defect: answer C is keyed on the Hindi 'wind velocity' reading, not on a literal measurement of force.

MPPSC-2012-005.correct_reasoning: Dengue is caused by a flavivirus (DENV) and transmitted to humans mainly by the bite of an infected female Aedes aegypti mosquito, which feeds during the day. The other options pair the wrong pathogen class or the wrong vector genus with dengue fever.

option_explanations.reason: Virus and female Aedes mosquito is right: dengue virus is a flavivirus and female Aedes aegypti is its principal daytime vector.
Bacteria and female Culex mosquito describes filariasis or Japanese encephalitis vectors, not dengue, which is viral and Aedes-borne.
Fungus and female Aedes mosquito halves the answer: the Aedes vector is correct, but dengue is viral rather than fungal in origin.
Protozoan and female Anopheles mosquito points to malaria, a Plasmodium parasite carried by Anopheles, not to dengue fever.

key_concepts: Female Aedes aegypti: daytime dengue vector
Anopheles and Plasmodium belong to malaria
revision_takeaways: Pair dengue with virus plus Aedes, malaria with protozoan plus Anopheles.

MPPSC-2012-006.correct_reasoning: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with roughly 200-plus times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing the oxygen carrying capacity of blood. Tissue hypoxia, not primary damage to digestion, liver or kidney, explains CO poisoning.

option_explanations.reason: Digestive activity is not the main target of carbon monoxide; the gas acts in the bloodstream rather than in the gastrointestinal tract.
Liver functioning may suffer secondarily from hypoxia, but carbon monoxide's defining toxic action is not hepatic metabolism.
Kidney functioning is not the primary site of carbon monoxide toxicity, though prolonged hypoxia can affect many organs.
Oxygen carrying capacity of blood is the correct focus: carboxyhaemoglobin blocks haemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites and shifts the dissociation curve.

revision_takeaways: Link carbon monoxide with carboxyhaemoglobin and oxygen transport, not with organ-specific digestion.

MPPSC-2012-007.correct_reasoning: Statics is the branch of mechanics that studies bodies in equilibrium, i.e. a state of rest with zero resultant force and moment. Dynamics deals with motion, statistics with data, so the state of rest is the branch's defining condition.

option_explanations.reason: State of motion belongs to dynamics or kinematics, the complementary branch that analyses moving bodies and their accelerations.
State of rest is correct: statics analyses forces on bodies at rest, where resultant force and resultant torque are both zero.
State of mind is a psychological phrase, not a mechanics term; statics has nothing to do with mental conditions.
Study of data is statistics, a different discipline whose similar-sounding name is a common exam trap against statics.

key_concepts: Statics: equilibrium of bodies at rest
Resultant force and moment equal zero in equilibrium
revision_takeaways: Do not confuse statics (mechanics of rest) with statistics (analysis of data).

MPPSC-2012-008.correct_reasoning: The IAU's 2006 definition requires a planet to orbit the Sun, be nearly round and clear its orbital neighbourhood; Pluto fails the third condition and was reclassified as a dwarf planet. Uranus, Neptune and Jupiter remain the eight-planet canon's outer planets.

option_explanations.reason: Uranus is an ice giant that satisfies all three IAU criteria and remains one of the eight planets after 2006.
Neptune also clears its orbital zone and retains full planetary status under the 2006 IAU resolution.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it has not cleared the Kuiper-belt neighbourhood of its orbit.
Jupiter is the largest planet and easily meets the orbit-clearing criterion, so it is unaffected by the IAU decision.

key_concepts: Pluto as a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt
revision_takeaways: Remember the IAU's 2006 demotion of Pluto and the orbit-clearing criterion behind it.

MPPSC-2012-009.correct_reasoning: World AIDS Day is observed every year on 1 December, a date chosen by the World Health Organization in 1988 to focus attention on HIV and AIDS. The other dates belong to other observances, not to the AIDS calendar.

option_explanations.reason: 12th January is National Youth Day in India, marking Swami Vivekananda's birthday, not the global AIDS observance.
1st April is commonly associated with April Fools' Day and, in India, with the start of the financial year, not AIDS Day.
1st May is International Workers' Day or Labour Day, whereas the AIDS campaign uses a December date.
1st December is correct: WHO designated it World AIDS Day in 1988 and the red ribbon is its symbol.

key_concepts: Red ribbon as the HIV/AIDS symbol
revision_takeaways: Fix 1 December for World AIDS Day and distinguish it from other January or May dates.

MPPSC-2012-010.correct_reasoning: NHPC is the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, a central public sector enterprise that builds and operates hydro and other power projects, so it belongs to electricity generation. MMTC trades minerals, MTNL provides telecom, and NCL mines coal.

option_explanations.reason: M.M.T.C. is the Minerals and Metals Trading Corporation, an export-import trading PSU rather than a power-generating company.
M.T.N.L. is Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited, a telecommunications service provider in Delhi and Mumbai, not a generator of electricity.
N.C.L. is Northern Coalfields Limited, a coal-mining subsidiary of Coal India, so it supplies fuel rather than generating power.
N.H.P.C. stands for National Hydroelectric Power Corporation and develops hydroelectric projects, which places it in electricity generation.

key_concepts: NCL: coal production under Coal India
revision_takeaways: Expand the abbreviations first: NHPC is the only generation company in this list.

MPPSC-2012-011.correct_reasoning: The Ajanta cave paintings and sculptures depict episodes from the Jataka tales, stories of the Buddha's earlier births, alongside Buddhist devotional imagery. They are Buddhist rock-cut caves in Maharashtra, not illustrations of the Ramayana, Mahabharata or Panchatantra.

option_explanations.reason: Ramayana scenes are common in other Indian temple art, but Ajanta's narrative panels are dominated by Buddhist Jataka stories.
Mahabharata episodes are not the textual source of Ajanta's painted narrative cycles, which follow Buddhist birth stories.
Jataka Stories is correct: Ajanta's murals illustrate the previous lives of the Buddha and Buddhist legends such as the Bodhisattva legends.
Panchtantra Stories are secular beast fables in Sanskrit, not the Buddhist scripture depicted in the Ajanta caves.

key_concepts: Ajanta caves: Buddhist rock-cut architecture in Maharashtra
Jataka tales: previous births of the Buddha
revision_takeaways: Ajanta equals Buddhism plus Jataka tales; Ellora mixes Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments.

MPPSC-2012-012.correct_reasoning: Both statements are accepted in standard exam material: Harappan sites yield some of the earliest cotton textile traces, and the civilisation is conventionally described as predominantly secular because no monumental temples or priest-ruler complexes dominate its remains. The identical UPSC 2011 item carries the answer 'Both 1 and 2'.

option_explanations.reason: (1) only is incomplete: cotton textiles from Mohenjo-daro and Mehrgarh are well attested, but the secular-character statement is also treated as correct in the standard key.
(2) only is incomplete because archaeological finds of cotton thread and cloth at Harappan sites independently establish the second statement as true.
Both (1) and (2) is correct: cotton was spun and woven in the Indus region and religious elements such as seals and the Great Bath did not dominate the urban layout.
Neither (1) nor (2) contradicts the archaeological record of cotton and the textbook characterisation of Harappan religion as non-monumental.

key_concepts: Harappan cotton: among the world's earliest cotton textiles
Great Bath and seals as limited religious evidence
UPSC 2011 question with both statements accepted
revision_takeaways: Treat statement 2 as a conventional textbook characterisation, not a measurable archaeological fact.

MPPSC-2012-013.correct_reasoning: The Tripitaka ('Three Baskets') is the canonical scripture of Buddhism, comprising Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitaka, compiled after the Buddha's death. Jains use the Agamas, Sikhs the Guru Granth Sahib and Hindus the Vedas, so Tripitaka belongs to Buddhists.

option_explanations.reason: Jains follow the Agamas and Tattvartha Sutra rather than the Tripitaka, so this option names the wrong religious community.
Buddhists is correct: the Tripitaka is the Pali Canon's threefold collection of discipline, discourses and higher doctrine.
Sikhs revere the Guru Granth Sahib as their eternal Guru, not the three baskets of Buddhist scripture.
Hindus base scripture on the Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas, so the Tripitaka is outside the Hindu canonical list.

key_concepts: Jain Agamas and Sikh Guru Granth Sahib
revision_takeaways: Map Tripitaka to Buddhists, Agamas to Jains and Guru Granth Sahib to Sikhs.

MPPSC-2012-014.correct_reasoning: Kalhana's Rajatarangini ('River of Kings'), written in Sanskrit in the twelfth century, is a verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir and is often called the nearest thing to a historical chronicle in classical India. It is not a Chandragupta biography, a lyric anthology or a Vijayanagara court history.

option_explanations.reason: Chandragupta's reign belongs to Mauryan history and sources such as the Arthashastra and Mudrarakshasa, not to Kalhana's Kashmiri chronicle.
Anthology of lyrics describes works like the Gita Govinda or Amaru Shataka, whereas Rajatarangini is a dynastic narrative poem.
History of Kashmir is correct: Kalhana's Rajatarangini records the rulers of Kashmir from mythic times to his own century.
Reign of Krishna Deva Raya belongs to Vijayanagara and the sixteenth century, centuries after Kalhana wrote in Kashmir.

key_concepts: Kashmir's dynastic chronicle in Sanskrit verse
Contrast with Vijayanagara and Mauryan sources
revision_takeaways: Rajatarangini equals Kalhana equals Kashmir, not a lyric anthology.

MPPSC-2012-015.correct_reasoning: No single answer can be keyed: the INA trial defence committee at the Red Fort included both Asaf Ali (option C) and Bhulabhai Desai (option D), with Desai as lead counsel and Nehru, Sapru and Katju among the nine advocates. An unauthenticated third-party key prints D, but both named lawyers were defence advocates, so the item stays unkeyed.

option_explanations.reason: Subhash Chandra Bose led the Azad Hind Fauj and was never an advocate in the Red Fort trials, so he cannot satisfy the question.
C. Rajagopalachari was not among the nine lawyers on the INA defence committee, which included Nehru, Sapru and Desai.
Asaf Ali was indeed one of the INA defence counsel, which makes this option factually supportable and creates the item's double-answer problem.
Bhulabhai Desai was the chief defence counsel and is the conventional answer, but option C is also true, so no honest single key can be given.

key_concepts: INA Defence Committee of nine counsel
Bhulabhai Desai as lead counsel, Asaf Ali as member
revision_takeaways: Record the defect rather than choosing between two genuine defence advocates.

MPPSC-2012-016.correct_reasoning: B. R. Ambedkar attended all three Round Table Conferences in London (1930-32) as a representative of the depressed classes, arguing for separate electorates and later signing the Poona Pact. Patel did not attend all three, Malviya attended the first two, so Ambedkar is the consistent attendee.

option_explanations.reason: Vallabhbhai Patel was not a participant in all three Round Table Conferences; Congress attended only the second session, and that too without this claim.
Madan Mohan Malviya attended the first and second conferences but not the third, so 'all three' does not fit him.
B.R. Ambedkar is correct: he was nominated to each of the three sessions and pressed for safeguards for the depressed classes.
None of the above is wrong because Ambedkar did attend all three, so a valid named option exists.

key_concepts: Ambedkar and the depressed classes' representation
revision_takeaways: Ambedkar is the standard answer for attendance at all three Round Table Conferences.

MPPSC-2012-017.correct_reasoning: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar founded the revolutionary society Abhinav Bharat in 1904 (originally Mitra Mela) in Maharashtra, inspired by Mazzini's Young Italy. Madan Lal Dhingra was a member, Jatindra Nath Mukherjee led Jugantar and Lala Hardayal the Ghadar Party, so Savarkar is the organiser.

option_explanations.reason: Jatindra Nath Mukherjee was associated with the Jugantar group in Bengal, not with founding Abhinav Bharat in western India.
Madan Lal Dhingra was an Abhinav Bharat member who assassinated Curzon Wyllie in London, but he did not organise the society.
Vinayak Damodar Savarkar is correct: he set up Mitra Mela, later renamed Abhinav Bharat, and drafted its revolutionary programme.
Lala Hardayal founded the Ghadar Party in North America, a separate revolutionary organisation with a different base.

key_concepts: Ghadar Party and Jugantar as distinct groups
revision_takeaways: Abhinav Bharat equals Savarkar; Ghadar equals Hardayal; Jugantar equals Mukherjee.

MPPSC-2012-018.correct_reasoning: Atal Bihari Vajpayee, as India's external affairs minister, became the first person to address the UN General Assembly in Hindi, in 1977. Swami Vivekananda never spoke at the UN and Shastri, though a Hindi advocate, did not deliver a UN address in Hindi, so Vajpayee is the first.

option_explanations.reason: Swami Vivekananda's famous 1893 speech was at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago, decades before the United Nations existed.
Lal Bahadur Shastri promoted Hindi but is not recorded as having delivered a UN General Assembly speech in Hindi.
Atal Bihari Bajpayee is correct: his 1977 UNGA address in Hindi is widely recorded as the first Hindi speech at the world body.
None of the above fails because Vajpayee's 1977 Hindi address is documented, so a listed option is correct.

key_concepts: Atal Bihari Vajpayee as External Affairs Minister
Distinguish the 1893 Chicago Parliament from the UN
revision_takeaways: Remember 1977 and Vajpayee for the first Hindi address to the UN General Assembly.

MPPSC-2012-019.correct_reasoning: Amir Khusrau is firmly associated with Alauddin Khalji's court: he wrote the Khazain-ul-Futuh (Tarikh-i-Alai) on that reign and served several Delhi sultans, while Britannica dates his death to 1325. Muhammad bin Tughlaq only acceded in 1325, so the Khalji association is the reliable one among these options.

option_explanations.reason: Allauddin Khilzi is correct: Khusrau was his court poet and chronicler, composing panegyrics and the Khazain-ul-Futuh on Khalji victories.
Muhammad Bin Tughlaq came to the throne in 1325, the year Khusrau died; the stronger courtly link is with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's Tughlaq Nama, not this reign.
Ibrahim Lodi ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1517, nearly two centuries after Khusrau's death, so the association is impossible.
Firoz Shah (Firuz Shah Tughlaq) reigned from 1351, also long after Khusrau died in 1325, so he cannot be the patron.

key_concepts: Chronology: Khalji, Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq
revision_takeaways: Use the poet's death date (1325) to test which sultan's reign he could actually have served.

MPPSC-2012-020.correct_reasoning: Mohenjo Daro is an archaeological site of the Indus Valley Civilisation in the Larkana district of Sindh province, Pakistan, on the right bank of the Indus. It lies outside India's Gujarat and Punjab and far from Afghanistan, so Sindh Province in Pakistan is correct.

option_explanations.reason: Gujarat state of India contains Harappan sites such as Dholavira and Lothal, but Mohenjo Daro itself is not in Gujarat.
Punjab state of India has sites like Ropar, whereas Mohenjo Daro lies in Pakistan's Sindh, not Indian Punjab.
Sindh Province in Pakistan is correct: Mohenjo Daro stands near the Indus in Larkana district and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Afghanistan has sites such as Shortugai linked to Harappan trade, but the major city of Mohenjo Daro is in Sindh.

key_concepts: Harappa in Pakistani Punjab, Lothal/Dholavira in Gujarat
revision_takeaways: Mohenjo Daro equals Sindh; Harappa equals Pakistani Punjab.

MPPSC-2012-021.correct_reasoning: Nagarjun Sagar Dam is built across the Krishna River on the border of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh; in the administrative framing of this 2013 paper the state named is Andhra Pradesh. The other three states are not on the Krishna at this dam site.

option_explanations.reason: Tamil Nadu's major dams include Mettur on the Kaveri, not Nagarjun Sagar on the Krishna, so this option is wrong.
Andhra Pradesh is correct in the paper's pre-bifurcation framing: Nagarjun Sagar is on the Krishna and its reservoir straddles the later Telangana border.
Karnataka has Krishna projects such as Almatti, but the Nagarjun Sagar dam itself is downstream, outside Karnataka.
Orissa (Odisha) is associated with the Mahanadi and Hirakud Dam, not with the Krishna River's Nagarjun Sagar project.

key_concepts: Nagarjun Sagar Dam on the Krishna River
Pre-2014 Andhra Pradesh and later Telangana
Hirakud on the Mahanadi as a comparison
revision_takeaways: Note the date-dependent state name: the 2013 paper predates Telangana's formation.

MPPSC-2012-022.correct_reasoning: The conventional exam answer is Uttar Pradesh, but this item stays unkeyed because the classification is genuinely contested: Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Himachal Pradesh are Himalayan states, while official UP material also places Shivalik/Dundwa foothills in northern Uttar Pradesh, which are part of the Outer Himalayas by geological definition.

option_explanations.reason: Uttarakhand contains Garhwal and Kumaon Himalaya and Nanda Devi, so it is unambiguously a Himalayan state and cannot be the exception.
Uttar Pradesh is the intended answer in exam convention, yet Saharanpur's Shivalik/Dundwa range is Outer Himalaya, so the option cannot be verified cleanly.
Sikkim lies in the Eastern Himalaya and contains Kangchenjunga, so it is certainly part of the Himalayan ranges.
Himachal Pradesh includes Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar and the Great Himalaya, so it too is unquestionably Himalayan.

key_concepts: Himalayan states: Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim
Shivalik/Dundwa outliers in northern Uttar Pradesh
revision_takeaways: Keep the item unkeyed: the exam convention and the Shivalik classification genuinely conflict.

MPPSC-2012-023.correct_reasoning: The Indian summer monsoon advances from the south-west over the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal toward the north-east of the subcontinent, driven by the land-sea thermal gradient and the shifted ITCZ. Options naming south-east or northward-only flow misstate both the source and destination.

option_explanations.reason: From South to North misses the defining westerly component: the monsoon arrives from the south-west, not the due south.
From South-west to South-east reverses the destination; the Arabian Sea branch moves inland and north-eastward, not back toward the south-east.
From South-east to South-west reverses the actual direction, confusing the retreating north-east monsoon with the incoming south-west monsoon.
From South-west to North-east is correct: the south-west monsoon crosses the Arabian Sea and advances up the peninsula and Gangetic plain.

key_concepts: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches
ITCZ shift and land-sea thermal contrast
revision_takeaways: South-west monsoon moves south-west to north-east; the winter reversal is north-east to south-west.

MPPSC-2012-024.correct_reasoning: Census of India 2011 provisional figures reported a national sex ratio of 940 females per 1,000 males, up from 933 in 2001. The adjacent numbers 935, 945 and 950 are plausible-looking distractors rather than the published provisional total.

option_explanations.reason: 935 is close to the 2001 figure of 933 but is not the 2011 provisional sex ratio released by the Registrar General.
940 is correct: provisional 2011 Census data gave 940 females per 1,000 males at the all-India level.
945 is a rounded value sometimes quoted for specific states or later estimates, not the national provisional figure.
950 exceeds the 2011 provisional total and would contradict the published 940 figure for India as a whole.

key_concepts: Sex ratio measured as females per 1,000 males
revision_takeaways: Memorise 940 for Census 2011 and 933 for Census 2001.

MPPSC-2012-025.correct_reasoning: Jim Corbett National Park (then Hailey National Park), established in 1936 in Uttarakhand, is India's first national park and later the first Project Tiger reserve. Kanha, Dudhwa and Rajaji were notified afterwards, so Corbett has chronological priority.

option_explanations.reason: Kanha National Park in Madhya Pradesh was notified in 1955, nearly two decades after Corbett, so it is not India's first national park.
Dudhwa National Park in Uttar Pradesh was established in 1977, long after the 1936 Corbett notification.
Rajaji National Park in Uttarakhand was created in 1983 by merging several sanctuaries, so it cannot precede Corbett.
Corbett National Park is correct: founded in 1936 as Hailey National Park, it is India's oldest national park.

revision_takeaways: Corbett equals India's first national park, 1936, Uttarakhand.

MPPSC-2012-026.correct_reasoning: Alaska is the 49th state of the United States of America, purchased from Russia in 1867 and admitted to the Union in 1959. It is geographically separated from the contiguous USA by Canada but is neither Canadian, Russian nor part of Greenland.

option_explanations.reason: Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, a separate Arctic island east of Canada, not the state containing Alaska.
United States of America is correct: Alaska was bought from Russia in 1867 and became the 49th US state in 1959.
Canada lies between Alaska and the lower 48 states, but Alaska itself was never Canadian territory.
Russia sold Alaska to the United States in 1867, so describing Alaska as part of Russia confuses the seller with the present sovereign.

revision_takeaways: Alaska equals USA; remember the 1867 purchase from Russia as the exam hook.

MPPSC-2012-027.correct_reasoning: The Andes run along the western edge of South America, stretching from Venezuela and Colombia down through Peru and Chile to Argentina, and form the world's longest continental mountain range. Australia, Europe and North America host different ranges such as the Great Dividing Range, Alps and Rockies.

option_explanations.reason: Australia's major range is the Great Dividing Range in the east, so the Andes cannot be placed in Australia.
Europe has the Alps, Pyrenees and Carpathians, not the Andes, which lie on a different continent and tectonic margin.
South America is correct: the Andes follow the Nazca-South American plate boundary from the tropics to Tierra del Fuego.
North America's western cordillera includes the Rockies and Sierra Nevada, which are distinct from the South American Andes.

key_concepts: Andes: western South America, longest continental range
Andean countries: Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, Colombia
revision_takeaways: Andes equals South America; Rockies equal North America.

MPPSC-2012-028.correct_reasoning: The Equator crosses Kenya, Indonesia and Brazil, but Mexico lies entirely north of it, between roughly 14 and 32 degrees north latitude. It is therefore the country in this list that the Equator does not pass through.

option_explanations.reason: Kenya is crossed by the Equator near Mount Kenya and the town of Nanyuki, so it cannot be the exception.
Mexico is correct as the exception: its southernmost point is still well north of 0 degrees latitude, so the Equator never crosses it.
Indonesia is crossed by the Equator through Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, so it is an equatorial country.
Brazil contains the Equator near the Amazon basin and Macapa, so it too is crossed by the line.

key_concepts: Mexico lies wholly in the Northern Hemisphere
revision_takeaways: Use latitude: Mexico is north of the Equator, while Brazil, Kenya and Indonesia straddle it.

MPPSC-2012-029.correct_reasoning: The conventional place nickname 'City of Canals' belongs to Venice, built on islands in a lagoon with canals in place of streets; Amsterdam is more often called the 'Venice of the North'. Travel sources occasionally use the phrase loosely for Amsterdam, so the nickname is a convention rather than an exclusive geographic fact, but C is the standard answer.

option_explanations.reason: Amsterdam has more than a hundred canals and is called the Venice of the North, but the stock epithet City of Canals is reserved for Venice.
Rome is famed for its seven hills, aqueducts and the Tiber, not for a canal network, so it is plainly wrong.
Venice is correct: its Grand Canal and lagoon islands make 'City of Canals' the standard geographic nickname used in exam keys.
Athens is associated with the Acropolis and the Aegean, not with canals, so this option is a straightforward distractor.

key_concepts: Venice: City of Canals, lagoon city
Nicknames are conventional, not exclusive properties
revision_takeaways: Note the ambiguity: Amsterdam also has canals, but the conventional nickname answer is Venice.

MPPSC-2012-030.correct_reasoning: Bhutan shares borders with Sikkim, West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, but not with Meghalaya, which lies south of Assam and borders Bangladesh. Meghalaya is therefore the state that does not share a border with Bhutan.

option_explanations.reason: Sikkim borders Bhutan on its eastern side near the Chumbi valley and Nathu La region, so it does share a border.
Meghalaya is correct: it borders Assam and Bangladesh and is separated from Bhutan by Assam, so it has no Bhutan boundary.
Arunachal Pradesh has a long northern border with Bhutan along the Himalayan foothills, so it is not the exception.
West Bengal's Darjeeling and Kalimpong areas touch Bhutan, so West Bengal does share a border with the kingdom.

key_concepts: Indian states bordering Bhutan: Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh
revision_takeaways: Remember the four Bhutan-bordering states; Meghalaya is the common trap.

MPPSC-2012-031.correct_reasoning: The Constituent Assembly was not elected on universal adult franchise: its members were chosen indirectly by provincial legislatures under the Cabinet Mission plan, with a restricted property-, tax- and education-based electorate. Statement C is therefore the incorrect one, while the committees, minority representation and the 1935 Act-based electoral scheme are accurate.

option_explanations.text: It worked with the help of a large number of committees, the most important among them being the Drafting Committee
